statement.p: Use the figure below to estimate the indicated derivatives, or state that they do not exist. If a derivative does not exist, enter dne in the answer blank. The graph of f(x) is black and has a sharp corner at x = 2. The graph of g(x) is blue.

p.em: (Enter dne for any derivative that does not exist.)

solution.p: Using the product rule, we know that h'(x) = f'(x) \cdot g(x) + f(x) \cdot g'(x). We use slope to compute the derivatives. Since f(x) is linear on the interval 0 \lt x \lt 2, we compute the slope of the line to see that f'(x) = 1 on this interval. Similarly, we compute the slope on the interval 2 \lt x \lt 4 to see that f'(x) = -1 there. Since f(x) has a corner at x = 2, we know that f'(2) does not exist. Similarly, g(x) is linear on the interval shown, and we see that the slope of g(x) on this interval is -0.25, so we have g'(x) = -0.25 on this interval.
B. We would like to say h'(2) = f'(2) \cdot g(2) + f(2) \cdot g'(2), but actually can't apply the product rule here, because f(x) has a corner at x = 2, and is therefore not differentiable there.

However, for these functions f(x) and g(x) the product rule does apply for all points to the left and right of x=2, and because the two functions are piecewise linear we can see that for x\lt 2, h'(x) = 0.5 and for x>2, h'(x) = -0.5. Thus h(x) has the same characteristic non-differentiability as f(x) at x=2, and we can say that h'(2) does not exist.
